question.text: What do yellow lines divide, and when may you cross a broken or a solid yellow line?

answer.text: Yellow lines divide traffic moving in opposite directions; a broken yellow line may be crossed to pass once the way is safe, while a solid yellow line should be crossed only to turn.

teaching.text: Yellow lines separate opposite directions; cross a broken one only to pass when it is safe, and a solid one only to turn. Remember: yellow splits opposite directions.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Yellow lines divide traffic moving in opposite directions; a broken yellow line may be crossed to pass once the way is safe, while a solid yellow line should be crossed only to turn.

question.text: What do white lines divide, and may you cross a broken or a solid white line?

answer.text: White lines divide lanes moving the same direction; you may cross a broken white line to change lanes when safe, but you should not cross a solid white line.

teaching.text: White lines separate lanes going your way; broken white may be crossed when safe, solid white should not be crossed. Remember: white splits same direction.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: White lines divide lanes moving the same direction; you may cross a broken white line to change lanes when safe, but you should not cross a solid white line.

question.text: Which lane should slower vehicles use on the highway?

answer.text: On the highway, slower vehicles should keep right, leaving the left lane for faster or passing traffic.

teaching.text: On the highway, slower traffic keeps right and the left lane is for faster or passing vehicles. Remember: slow traffic keeps right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On the highway, slower vehicles should keep right, leaving the left lane for faster or passing traffic.

question.text: How many lanes may you change at once, and what must you do first?

answer.text: Change only one lane at a time, and give a proper signal before any turn or lane change.

teaching.text: Move over one lane at a time, and signal before every turn or lane change. Remember: one lane, signal first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Change only one lane at a time, and give a proper signal before any turn or lane change.

question.text: What are the steps before changing lanes?

answer.text: Before changing lanes, check the lane ahead, check mirrors for anyone about to pass you, glance over your shoulder at the blind spot, signal, then move over smoothly.

teaching.text: A safe lane change runs in order: look ahead, check mirrors, glance at the blind spot, signal, then move smoothly. Remember: ahead, mirrors, shoulder, signal, move.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before changing lanes, check the lane ahead, check mirrors for anyone about to pass you, glance over your shoulder at the blind spot, signal, then move over smoothly.

question.text: What does weaving in and out of lanes do to your crash risk?

answer.text: Weaving in and out of lanes greatly raises the risk of a crash.

teaching.text: Darting from lane to lane greatly increases your chance of a crash. Remember: weaving raises crash risk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Weaving in and out of lanes greatly raises the risk of a crash.

question.text: How far ahead of an oncoming vehicle must you be back on the right after passing?

answer.text: Before passing, make sure the passing lane is clear, because you must be back on the right side of the road at least one hundred feet before any oncoming vehicle.

teaching.text: Only start a pass when the lane is clear enough to be back on the right one hundred feet before any oncoming vehicle. Remember: back before oncoming traffic.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before passing, make sure the passing lane is clear, because you must be back on the right side of the road at least one hundred feet before any oncoming vehicle.

question.text: When may you move back after passing a vehicle?

answer.text: Stay in the passing lane until the vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror, then signal before moving back.

teaching.text: Hold the passing lane until you can see the passed car in your rearview mirror, then signal and move back. Remember: see it in the mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay in the passing lane until the vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror, then signal before moving back.

question.text: Which markings, signs and road features make passing illegal?

answer.text: Passing is illegal where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, where a No Passing Zone pennant or a Do Not Pass sign is posted, on or near a curve, and near the crest of a hill.

teaching.text: Do not pass where a solid yellow is on your side, where no-passing signs are posted, near curves or near a hill crest. Remember: solid yellow, signs, curves, crests.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing is illegal where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, where a No Passing Zone pennant or a Do Not Pass sign is posted, on or near a curve, and near the crest of a hill.

question.text: Near which places is passing illegal within a set distance?

answer.text: Passing is also illegal within one hundred feet of an intersection, a railroad crossing, a bridge, a viaduct or a tunnel.

teaching.text: Stay behind slower traffic within one hundred feet of intersections, railroad crossings, bridges, viaducts and tunnels. Remember: no passing near crossings.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing is also illegal within one hundred feet of an intersection, a railroad crossing, a bridge, a viaduct or a tunnel.

question.text: What should you do when another vehicle is passing you on the left?

answer.text: When another vehicle is passing you on the left, let it pass safely and do not speed up.

teaching.text: When someone passes you, let them complete it safely and keep your speed steady. Remember: let them pass, hold speed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When another vehicle is passing you on the left, let it pass safely and do not speed up.

question.text: Which lane should you be in to turn left or turn right?

answer.text: To turn left, get into the far-left lane for your direction well ahead of the turn, and to turn right use the far-right lane, signaling and yielding to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians.

teaching.text: Set up turns early: far-left lane to turn left, far-right lane to turn right, with a signal and a yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians. Remember: far lane for your turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To turn left, get into the far-left lane for your direction well ahead of the turn, and to turn right use the far-right lane, signaling and yielding to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians.

question.text: Which turn signal is safest, and when may hand signals be used?

answer.text: Built-in lighted turn signals are the safest signal; hand signals may be used if a lighted signal fails, but not on a driving skills exam.

teaching.text: Use your car's lighted signals; hand signals are only a backup if a light fails, and they are not allowed on the skills exam. Remember: lights first, hands as backup.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Built-in lighted turn signals are the safest signal; hand signals may be used if a lighted signal fails, but not on a driving skills exam.

question.text: What must you never do in a center left-turn lane, and what should you watch for?

answer.text: Never use a center left-turn lane to pass, and watch for oncoming drivers entering it to turn left in front of you.

teaching.text: The center left-turn lane is never a passing lane, and oncoming drivers may pull into it to turn in front of you. Remember: center lane never for passing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never use a center left-turn lane to pass, and watch for oncoming drivers entering it to turn left in front of you.

question.text: How are center left-turn lanes usually marked?

answer.text: Center lanes reserved for left turns are usually marked with CENTER LANE ONLY signs or pavement arrows, though some have neither.

teaching.text: Look for CENTER LANE ONLY signs or pavement arrows, though some center turn lanes have neither. Remember: center lane only signs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Center lanes reserved for left turns are usually marked with CENTER LANE ONLY signs or pavement arrows, though some have neither.

question.text: Where must you never make a U-turn?

answer.text: Never make a U-turn on a curve, near the crest of a hill, or on an interstate, where you should go to the next exit and come back the other way.

teaching.text: Skip U-turns on curves, near hill crests and on interstates; on an interstate, take the next exit and come back. Remember: no U-turns on curves, crests.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never make a U-turn on a curve, near the crest of a hill, or on an interstate, where you should go to the next exit and come back the other way.

question.text: How does a median U-turn or J-turn intersection handle left turns?

answer.text: At a median U-turn or J-turn intersection, the left turn is banned at the intersection itself, so drivers go through and make a U-turn at a median opening ahead.

teaching.text: At a median U-turn intersection, go through and make the U-turn at the median opening ahead instead of turning left. Remember: go through, then U-turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a median U-turn or J-turn intersection, the left turn is banned at the intersection itself, so drivers go through and make a U-turn at a median opening ahead.

question.text: Who goes first at an all-way stop, and who yields when two arrive together?

answer.text: At an all-way stop the first vehicle to stop goes first; when two arrive together the vehicle on the left yields, and if there is any doubt it is better to yield.

teaching.text: At an all-way stop, the first car to stop goes first, the car on the left yields in a tie, and when unsure, yield. Remember: first stopped, first gone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At an all-way stop the first vehicle to stop goes first; when two arrive together the vehicle on the left yields, and if there is any doubt it is better to yield.

question.text: Which way does roundabout traffic move, and who yields when entering?

answer.text: Traffic in a roundabout moves counterclockwise and enters or leaves only by right turns, and entering traffic always yields to traffic already circulating.

teaching.text: Roundabouts run counterclockwise, you enter and leave with right turns, and you yield to traffic already circling. Remember: counterclockwise, entering yields.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Traffic in a roundabout moves counterclockwise and enters or leaves only by right turns, and entering traffic always yields to traffic already circulating.

question.text: How does a roundabout differ from a traffic circle?

answer.text: A roundabout carries only counterclockwise traffic, while a traffic circle may carry traffic in both directions and may use stop signs instead of yield signs on its approaches.

teaching.text: Unlike a roundabout, a traffic circle may run both ways and may use stop signs at its entries. Remember: circles may run both ways.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A roundabout carries only counterclockwise traffic, while a traffic circle may carry traffic in both directions and may use stop signs instead of yield signs on its approaches.

question.text: Whom must you yield to in a multi-lane roundabout, and which truck yields to which?

answer.text: In a multi-lane roundabout, yield to large vehicles going through at the same time, and when two large trucks are side by side the one in the right lane yields to the one in the left lane.

teaching.text: In a multi-lane roundabout, give way to large vehicles, and when two big trucks are side by side, the right-lane truck yields. Remember: yield to big vehicles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a multi-lane roundabout, yield to large vehicles going through at the same time, and when two large trucks are side by side the one in the right lane yields to the one in the left lane.

question.text: When should you choose your lane in a multi-lane roundabout?

answer.text: In a multi-lane roundabout, pick your lane before entering and do not change lanes while circulating.

teaching.text: Choose your roundabout lane before you enter and stay in it while circulating. Remember: pick your lane before entering.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In a multi-lane roundabout, pick your lane before entering and do not change lanes while circulating.

question.text: What should you do when the driver ahead signals or slows for a turn?

answer.text: When the driver ahead signals a turn or slows as if to turn, slow down and be ready to stop.

teaching.text: When the car ahead signals or slows to turn, slow down and be ready to stop. Remember: slow and be ready.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When the driver ahead signals a turn or slows as if to turn, slow down and be ready to stop.

question.text: How does going over the speed limit affect steering, stopping and crashes?

answer.text: Going over the speed limit reduces your ability to steer around curves and objects, lengthens emergency stopping distance and makes crashes more severe.

teaching.text: Speeding cuts your ability to steer around curves and objects, adds to stopping distance and makes crashes more severe. Remember: speed weakens control.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Going over the speed limit reduces your ability to steer around curves and objects, lengthens emergency stopping distance and makes crashes more severe.

question.text: What are the rural interstate limits for passenger vehicles and heavy trucks?

answer.text: On rural interstates, passenger vehicles may not go over seventy miles per hour, and trucks with a declared gross weight over twenty-six thousand pounds may not go over sixty-five, or the lower posted limit.

teaching.text: Rural interstates allow seventy for passenger vehicles and sixty-five for trucks over twenty-six thousand pounds, unless a lower limit is posted. Remember: seventy cars, sixty-five trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On rural interstates, passenger vehicles may not go over seventy miles per hour, and trucks with a declared gross weight over twenty-six thousand pounds may not go over sixty-five, or the lower posted limit.

question.text: What is the limit on a rural state divided highway?

answer.text: On a rural state divided highway, the limit is sixty miles per hour or the posted limit.

teaching.text: On a rural state divided highway, the default limit is sixty unless posted. Remember: sixty on rural divided.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On a rural state divided highway, the limit is sixty miles per hour or the posted limit.

question.text: What is the limit on urban interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads?

answer.text: In urban areas of at least fifty thousand people, the limit is fifty-five miles per hour on urban interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads unless a different limit is posted.

teaching.text: In urban areas of fifty thousand or more, interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads default to fifty-five. Remember: fifty-five in town.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In urban areas of at least fifty thousand people, the limit is fifty-five miles per hour on urban interstates, non-divided state highways and county roads unless a different limit is posted.

question.text: What are the usual limits in urban residential areas and in alleys?

answer.text: Most urban residential areas have a thirty miles per hour limit and alleys a fifteen miles per hour limit unless another limit is posted.

teaching.text: Residential streets usually default to thirty and alleys to fifteen, unless posted. Remember: thirty homes, fifteen alleys.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Most urban residential areas have a thirty miles per hour limit and alleys a fifteen miles per hour limit unless another limit is posted.

question.text: When do school zone limits commonly apply?

answer.text: School zone limits commonly apply from seven a.m. to four thirty p.m. Monday through Friday or whenever the school beacons flash, and local authorities may set lower limits whenever children are present.

teaching.text: School zone limits commonly apply on weekday school hours or whenever the beacons flash, and local authorities may set lower limits when children are present. Remember: school days or flashing beacons.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: School zone limits commonly apply from seven a.m. to four thirty p.m. Monday through Friday or whenever the school beacons flash, and local authorities may set lower limits whenever children are present.

question.text: What are the school bus speed limits?

answer.text: A school bus off interstates and state highways is limited to forty miles per hour, while on an interstate or highway its limit is sixty miles per hour or the posted limit.

teaching.text: School buses are held to forty off interstates and state highways, and to sixty or the posted limit on them. Remember: forty local, sixty highway.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A school bus off interstates and state highways is limited to forty miles per hour, while on an interstate or highway its limit is sixty miles per hour or the posted limit.

question.text: How much lower is a work site speed limit, and when does it apply?

answer.text: A work site speed limit is always at least ten miles per hour below the area's normal maximum, and some apply only while flashing while others apply at all times.

teaching.text: Work site limits sit at least ten below the normal maximum, and some apply only while flashing while others apply all the time. Remember: work zones at least ten lower.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A work site speed limit is always at least ten miles per hour below the area's normal maximum, and some apply only while flashing while others apply at all times.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: work zones at least ten lower

question.text: When is driving at or above the posted limit even more dangerous?

answer.text: Driving at or above the posted limit is even more dangerous in bad weather, on icy roads, with worn tires, with unsafe vehicle conditions or when physically impaired.

teaching.text: Bad weather, ice, worn tires, unsafe vehicles or physical impairment make driving at the limit even more dangerous. Remember: bad conditions, slow down.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Driving at or above the posted limit is even more dangerous in bad weather, on icy roads, with worn tires, with unsafe vehicle conditions or when physically impaired.

question.text: How far behind the vehicle ahead should you stay, and how do you measure it?

answer.text: Stay at least two to three seconds behind the vehicle ahead, counting from when it passes a fixed object until you pass the same object.

teaching.text: Count two to three seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed object until you reach it. Remember: two to three seconds back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stay at least two to three seconds behind the vehicle ahead, counting from when it passes a fixed object until you pass the same object.

question.text: About how many feet does a vehicle cover each second at fifty-five miles per hour?

answer.text: At fifty-five miles per hour a vehicle covers about eighty point seven feet each second, compared with about fifty-one point three feet at thirty-five and one hundred two point seven feet at seventy.

teaching.text: At fifty-five you cover about eighty point seven feet every second, which is why distance ahead matters. Remember: about eighty feet per second.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At fifty-five miles per hour a vehicle covers about eighty point seven feet each second, compared with about fifty-one point three feet at thirty-five and one hundred two point seven feet at seventy.

question.text: What affects a vehicle's ability to stop?

answer.text: Stopping ability depends on vehicle weight, brakes, tires, pavement condition and slickness, and the grade of the road.

teaching.text: How fast you can stop depends on weight, brakes, tires, pavement and its slickness, and the road's grade. Remember: weight, brakes, tires, pavement, grade.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Stopping ability depends on vehicle weight, brakes, tires, pavement condition and slickness, and the grade of the road.

question.text: How do you recover from a skid with conventional brakes?

answer.text: To recover from a skid, ease off the gas and avoid steering too far; with conventional brakes, steer smoothly in the direction the rear of the car is sliding.

teaching.text: In a skid, ease off the gas and do not oversteer; with conventional brakes, steer smoothly toward where the rear is sliding. Remember: steer where the rear slides.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To recover from a skid, ease off the gas and avoid steering too far; with conventional brakes, steer smoothly in the direction the rear of the car is sliding.

question.text: How do you brake in a skid with anti-lock brakes?

answer.text: With anti-lock brakes, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer normally, without pumping; pedal vibration or noise means ABS is working.

teaching.text: With anti-lock brakes, press firmly and keep pressing while you steer, never pumping, and expect vibration or noise. Remember: press firm, never pump.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: With anti-lock brakes, keep firm, continuous pressure on the brake pedal and steer normally, without pumping; pedal vibration or noise means ABS is working.

question.text: What changes the skid technique: drive type or brake type?

answer.text: The skid steps are the same for front-wheel-drive and rear-wheel-drive cars; what changes the technique is whether the car has conventional or anti-lock brakes.

teaching.text: Front-wheel or rear-wheel drive does not change the skid steps, but the type of brakes does. Remember: brakes decide the technique.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The skid steps are the same for front-wheel-drive and rear-wheel-drive cars; what changes the technique is whether the car has conventional or anti-lock brakes.

question.text: What should you do if your vehicle runs off the road?

answer.text: If your vehicle runs off the road, do not jerk back onto the pavement; ease off the gas and steer back gradually when it is safe, since overcorrecting is a common cause of rollovers.

teaching.text: If you drop off the pavement, do not jerk back; ease off the gas and steer back gradually when it is safe. Remember: ease back, no jerking.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If your vehicle runs off the road, do not jerk back onto the pavement; ease off the gas and steer back gradually when it is safe, since overcorrecting is a common cause of rollovers.

question.text: How big a share of passenger vehicle deaths are rollovers, and what helps avoid them?

answer.text: Rollover crashes make up nearly one-third of passenger vehicle deaths; keeping control of the vehicle is the biggest factor in avoiding one, and badly inflated or worn tires undermine that control.

teaching.text: Rollovers cause nearly one-third of passenger vehicle deaths, and keeping control matters most; tires can lose up to one pound per square inch a month, so check pressure cold against the door-jamb sticker, and use the penny test, where some of Lincoln's head covered by tread means a legal and safe amount. Remember: control and good tires prevent rollovers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rollover crashes make up nearly one-third of passenger vehicle deaths; keeping control of the vehicle is the biggest factor in avoiding one, and badly inflated or worn tires undermine that control.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: control and good tires prevent rollovers

question.text: Where are rollovers more likely?

answer.text: Rollovers are more likely on undivided two-way roads or divided roads without barriers, and a car leaving a rural road can roll when it hits a ditch, an embankment or soft soil.

teaching.text: Rollovers happen more often on undivided two-way roads and barrier-free divided roads, and when a car leaving a rural road hits a ditch, embankment or soft soil. Remember: undivided roads and ditches.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rollovers are more likely on undivided two-way roads or divided roads without barriers, and a car leaving a rural road can roll when it hits a ditch, an embankment or soft soil.

question.text: How does fuel use change as speed rises?

answer.text: Fuel use climbs steadily above forty-five miles per hour, and cars and light trucks use roughly fifty percent more fuel at seventy-five than at fifty-five.

teaching.text: Fuel use rises steadily above forty-five, about fifty percent more at seventy-five than at fifty-five. Remember: faster burns more fuel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Fuel use climbs steadily above forty-five miles per hour, and cars and light trucks use roughly fifty percent more fuel at seventy-five than at fifty-five.

question.text: How do several short cold-start trips compare with one longer trip for fuel?

answer.text: Several short trips from a cold start can burn twice as much fuel as one longer trip covering the same distance.

teaching.text: Combine errands, because several short cold-start trips can use twice the fuel of one longer trip. Remember: combine trips, save fuel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Several short trips from a cold start can burn twice as much fuel as one longer trip covering the same distance.

question.text: Which road surfaces can freeze first, and how should you treat snowplows?

answer.text: Ramps, bridges and overpasses can freeze before the rest of the road, and drivers should keep a safe distance behind snowplows.

teaching.text: Bridges, ramps and overpasses can ice over first, and you should stay well back from snowplows. Remember: bridges freeze first.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Ramps, bridges and overpasses can freeze before the rest of the road, and drivers should keep a safe distance behind snowplows.

question.text: How should you prepare your car for very cold weather?

answer.text: In very cold weather, let the engine warm up, keep a full gas tank so the heater can run if stranded, and clear snow from headlights and taillights often.

teaching.text: Before cold-weather driving, warm the engine, keep the tank full for the heater if stranded, and keep your lights clear of snow. Remember: warm up, full tank.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In very cold weather, let the engine warm up, keep a full gas tank so the heater can run if stranded, and clear snow from headlights and taillights often.

question.text: How does speed affect hydroplaning, and what should you do after driving through puddles?

answer.text: Hydroplaning gets worse as speed rises; after driving through puddles, pump the brakes to dry them.

teaching.text: The faster you go, the worse hydroplaning gets, and a few brake pumps after puddles help dry the brakes. Remember: pump brakes after puddles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Hydroplaning gets worse as speed rises; after driving through puddles, pump the brakes to dry them.

question.text: What should you do about roads covered by water, and if your car stalls in a flood?

answer.text: Never drive where water covers the road, and if your car stalls in a flooded area leave it as soon as possible.

teaching.text: Water over the road means turn around, and a car stalled in a flood should be left as soon as possible. Remember: never drive into water.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive where water covers the road, and if your car stalls in a flooded area leave it as soon as possible.

question.text: Why should you never drive around barricades during flash flooding?

answer.text: Flash flooding kills more people than any other roadway weather event each year, so never drive around barricades or past road closed signs.

teaching.text: Flash floods are the deadliest roadway weather event, so never go around barricades or road closed signs. Remember: floods are the deadliest.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Flash flooding kills more people than any other roadway weather event each year, so never drive around barricades or past road closed signs.

question.text: Which headlights should you use in fog, and what if visibility drops to near zero?

answer.text: In fog, drive slowly with low beams rather than high beams, and if visibility drops to near zero pull as far off the road as you can and stop.

teaching.text: In fog, slow down and use low beams, and if you can barely see, pull far off the road and stop. Remember: low beams in fog.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: In fog, drive slowly with low beams rather than high beams, and if visibility drops to near zero pull as far off the road as you can and stop.

question.text: When are headlights required, and when must you dim to low beams?

answer.text: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and whenever visibility is under five hundred feet, and you must dim to low beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle or within two hundred feet behind another vehicle.

teaching.text: Turn on headlights from sunset to sunrise or when visibility is under five hundred feet, and dim for oncoming cars within five hundred feet or within two hundred feet behind another car. Remember: dim at five hundred facing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Headlights are required from sunset to sunrise and whenever visibility is under five hundred feet, and you must dim to low beams within five hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle or within two hundred feet behind another vehicle.

question.text: What distance applies for low beams when facing traffic, and when following?

answer.text: The low-beam rule uses five hundred feet for an oncoming vehicle but only two hundred feet when you are following another vehicle.

teaching.text: Two distances: five hundred feet for an oncoming car, two hundred feet for a car you are following. Remember: five hundred facing, two hundred following.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The low-beam rule uses five hundred feet for an oncoming vehicle but only two hundred feet when you are following another vehicle.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: five hundred facing, two hundred following

question.text: How can you avoid the glare of oncoming headlights at night?

answer.text: To avoid the glare of oncoming headlights at night, do not look straight into them; focus on the right side of the road instead.

teaching.text: Keep your eyes off oncoming headlights and on the right side of the road to avoid glare. Remember: eyes to the right edge.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: To avoid the glare of oncoming headlights at night, do not look straight into them; focus on the right side of the road instead.

question.text: Which age group is at the highest risk of drowsy driving?

answer.text: Young adults aged sixteen to twenty-nine are at the highest risk of drowsy driving, accounting for sixty-four percent of fatigue-related crashes.

teaching.text: Drivers aged sixteen to twenty-nine are most at risk of drowsy driving, and studies cited in the manual say eighteen hours without sleep impairs a driver as much as a point zero eight BAC. Remember: young adults at highest risk.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Young adults aged sixteen to twenty-nine are at the highest risk of drowsy driving, accounting for sixty-four percent of fatigue-related crashes.

question.text: What are warning signs of drowsiness?

answer.text: Warning signs of drowsiness include yawning or heavy eyelids, not remembering the last few miles, missing exits, drifting onto rumble strips and failing to hold a steady speed.

teaching.text: Watch for yawning, heavy eyelids, forgotten miles, missed exits, rumble strips and wandering speed. Remember: yawns, drifting, missed exits.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Warning signs of drowsiness include yawning or heavy eyelids, not remembering the last few miles, missing exits, drifting onto rumble strips and failing to hold a steady speed.

question.text: What does Indiana law say about using a phone while driving?

answer.text: Indiana law bans using a telecommunications device while driving unless it is hands-free or you are calling nine one one in a real emergency.

teaching.text: Indiana law allows phone use while driving only hands-free, or to call nine-one-one in a real emergency. Remember: hands-free or emergency only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Indiana law bans using a telecommunications device while driving unless it is hands-free or you are calling nine one one in a real emergency.

question.text: How long does reading or sending a text take your eyes off the road?

answer.text: Reading or sending a text takes your eyes off the road for five seconds, which at fifty-five miles per hour is like driving a football field blind.

teaching.text: One text takes your eyes off the road for five seconds, like crossing a football field blind at fifty-five. Remember: five seconds blind.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Reading or sending a text takes your eyes off the road for five seconds, which at fifty-five miles per hour is like driving a football field blind.

question.text: What share of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving, and what counts?

answer.text: About one-third of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving, meaning crashes caused by aggressive driving, disregarding a signal or speeding.

teaching.text: Dangerous driving, meaning aggressive driving, disregarding a signal or speeding, causes about one-third of Indiana traffic deaths. Remember: a third from dangerous driving.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: About one-third of Indiana traffic deaths come from dangerous driving, meaning crashes caused by aggressive driving, disregarding a signal or speeding.

question.text: When does Indiana law consider a driver to be driving aggressively?

answer.text: Under Indiana law, a driver is driving aggressively when at least three listed acts, such as tailgating, failure to yield or unnecessary horn use, happen during one episode of continuous driving.

teaching.text: Three listed acts such as tailgating, failing to yield or needless honking in one continuous drive make aggressive driving under Indiana law. Remember: three acts make aggression.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Under Indiana law, a driver is driving aggressively when at least three listed acts, such as tailgating, failure to yield or unnecessary horn use, happen during one episode of continuous driving.

question.text: How should you adjust for gravel roads?

answer.text: On gravel, traction is lower, so slow down earlier before turns and stops to avoid skidding.

teaching.text: Gravel gives less grip, so brake earlier for turns and stops. Remember: gravel means slow early.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On gravel, traction is lower, so slow down earlier before turns and stops to avoid skidding.

question.text: What should you do before the crest of a steep hill?

answer.text: Before the crest of a steep hill, slow down, keep to the right and watch for oncoming vehicles, and never try to pass there.

teaching.text: Approaching a steep hill crest, slow down, keep right, watch for oncoming cars and never pass. Remember: slow, keep right, no pass.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Before the crest of a steep hill, slow down, keep to the right and watch for oncoming vehicles, and never try to pass there.

question.text: Which headlights should you use on dusty dirt roads?

answer.text: On dusty dirt roads, use low beam headlights so other drivers can see you.

teaching.text: On dusty dirt roads, switch on your low beam headlights so other drivers can see you. Remember: low beams in dust.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: On dusty dirt roads, use low beam headlights so other drivers can see you.

question.text: How should you enter an interstate, and who must yield?

answer.text: When entering an interstate, stay right and build speed in the acceleration lane; drivers already on the interstate should make room, but entering drivers must yield to them.

teaching.text: Use the acceleration lane to reach speed, then yield to interstate traffic, which should make room for you. Remember: speed up, then yield in.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When entering an interstate, stay right and build speed in the acceleration lane; drivers already on the interstate should make room, but entering drivers must yield to them.

question.text: What should you do if you miss an interstate exit?

answer.text: If you miss an interstate exit, drive on to the next one; backing up is unsafe, and only emergency or highway maintenance vehicles may U-turn across the median.

teaching.text: Missed your exit? Take the next one; backing up is unsafe and only emergency or maintenance vehicles may cross the median. Remember: missed exit, take the next.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: If you miss an interstate exit, drive on to the next one; backing up is unsafe, and only emergency or highway maintenance vehicles may U-turn across the median.

question.text: When may you stop or park on an interstate shoulder?

answer.text: Do not stop or park on an interstate shoulder except for an emergency or a disabled vehicle.

teaching.text: Stop on an interstate shoulder only for an emergency or a disabled vehicle. Remember: shoulders for emergencies only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Do not stop or park on an interstate shoulder except for an emergency or a disabled vehicle.

question.text: Which lanes must trucks stay in on interstates?

answer.text: Trucks must stay in the right lane where an interstate has two lanes each way and in the right two lanes where it has three or more.

teaching.text: Trucks keep to the right lane on two-lane interstate sections and the right two lanes where there are three or more. Remember: trucks keep to the right.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks must stay in the right lane where an interstate has two lanes each way and in the right two lanes where it has three or more.

hooks_spoken: Yellow lines divide opposite directions and white lines divide the same direction; change one lane at a time with a signal.
Never pass on a solid yellow on your side, near curves or crests, or within one hundred feet of intersections and crossings.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of lanes and passing. Yellow lines divide opposite directions and white lines divide the same direction; change one lane at a time with a signal. hooks_spoken: At an all-way stop the first to stop goes first, and when two arrive together the driver on the left yields.
In a roundabout, travel counterclockwise and yield to traffic already circulating.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of turns and intersections. At an all-way stop the first to stop goes first, and when two arrive together the driver on the left yields. In a roundabout, travel counterclockwise and yield to traffic already circulating. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Seventy on rural interstates, sixty on rural divided highways, fifty-five in urban areas, thirty residential, fifteen alleys.
Stay at least two to three seconds behind the vehicle ahead.

hooks_spoken: With conventional brakes steer where the rear slides; with anti-lock brakes press firmly and do not pump.
If you run off the road, ease off the gas and steer back gradually.

hooks_spoken: Use low beams in fog, and dim within five hundred feet of oncoming traffic or two hundred feet when following.
Never drive where water covers the road, and use the phone only hands-free or for an emergency call.

hooks_spoken: Three listed acts in one episode make aggressive driving.
Enter the interstate yielding to traffic on it, and if you miss an exit, drive on to the next one.
